newsitem.title: UK: Branson - a hippie entrepreneur seeking adventure.
newsitem.headline: Branson - a hippie entrepreneur seeking adventure.

text.p: Millionaire businessman Richard Branson, whose attempt to fly round the world in a balloon ended in failure on Wednesday, is a former hippie whose fondness for schoolboyish pranks belies a brilliant business brain.

Often lost for words in private, Branson has become one of Britain's best known faces, and his attempt to be the first person to circle the globe in a balloon combined a taste for adventure with an undying desire to promote his Virgin Group.
The attempt had to be aborted because of technical problems, with the balloon landing in Algeria on Wednesday morning, less than 24 hours after it left Morocco. No one was injured.
Branson always recognised the dangers, but the temptation to complete what he calls "the last great aviation record and adventure left on earth" proved irresistible.
He decided to go ahead with the latest expedition in spite of the objections of his family.

He publicly promised his wife Joan he would give up this mode of transport six years ago after a successful crossing of the Pacific with balloon designer Per Lindstrand only narrowly avoided disaster, crash-landing on a frozen lake in Canada.
"I want to look back and think I've lived a full life. I wouldn't be the person I am if I didn't do these things. My wife knows this," he said recently.
Famous for his casual clothes, the 46-year-old "grinning pullover", as he was once dubbed, enjoys wide popularity in Britain as the acceptable face of capitalism.

Opinion polls have variously voted him in recent years as a possible candidate for president if Britain abolished the monarchy, as an ideal role model by young people, and as Britain's most admired businessman.
He started his first business venture at the age of 16 publishing a student magazine and soon after dropped out of his privileged private education at Stowe public school.

Although the magazine venture proved short-lived his attempts to sell advertising space put him onto the idea of selling records by mail order and two years later Virgin Mail-Order was born. Shops and a successful record company followed in quick succession.

The big breakthrough came in 1973 with the launch of the Virgin Records label with Mike Oldfield's "Tubular Bells", which sold over five million copies. Other big acts were to follow, including Genesis, The Sex Pistols, Phil Collins, Boy George, Paula Abdul, Janet Jackson and the Rolling Stones.

Branson has since developed a diversified consumer goods and entertainment group with sales of nearly 2.0 billion pounds ($3.4 billion) a year and a wide range of interests including air and rail services, nightclubs and hotels, drinks, books and financial services, all bearing the Virgin brand name.

In the process he has amassed a huge personal fortune, boosted in 1992 with the sale of Virgin Records to Thorn EMI for 560 million pounds, a move which he said was prompted by his determination to have a full war chest to nurture his fledgling airline, Virgin Atlantic Airways.
The investment paid off and Branson was front page news in 1993 after winning a celebrated libel case against his much bigger rival British Airways over allegations of dirty tricks.

Branson extracted a humbling apology and payment of a record libel settlement of 610,000 pounds by BA and gained the additional satisfaction of seeing BA's veteran chairman Lord King retire early in the aftermath of the affair.
King admitted that Branson's casual dress of open-necked shirts and woolly jumpers and his practical jokes made it difficult for him to take his accusations seriously.

"I underestimated him," King was reported as saying after the dirty tricks case in 1993. "If Richard Branson had worn a pair of steel-rimmed glasses, a double-breasted suit and shaved off his beard, I would have taken him seriously."

When he launched his airline in 1984, the maiden flight from London to New York featured pop entertainment, spoon-bending by Uri Geller, food from the exclusive restaurant Maxim's and Branson himself popping out of the pilot's cabin wearing goggles and a dashing uniform complete with silver braid epaulettes.
Branson made his first attempt to enter record books in 1985 by trying to make the fastest-ever crossing by boat of the Atlantic.
That time his powerboat capsized 140 miles off the British coast and he was rescued by helicopter but the following year he achieved his aim with Virgin Atlantic Challenger II.
Despite an eight-hour hold-up at sea with fuel trouble he knocked two hours and nine minutes off the old record of three days, 10 hours and 40 minutes held by the liner United States.

Then in July 1987 he completed a record-breaking Atlantic crossing by hot-air balloon from Maine to Northern Ireland in one-and-a-half days and made more headlines when his balloon had to be rescued from the sea. ($=0.5904 Pound)
